passage: Creche note, Tuesday. Around midday, Farhan, two, began rubbing his eyes with both fists and tugging his left ear. He also pressed his face into my shoulder. I didn't decide from one sign. It was just before nap time, he had eaten his lunch well, he felt cool to touch, and the room had been noisy since morning. I took him to the quiet corner and he slept. If the ear-tugging keeps going or worries us, I will tell his parents to see the doctor. 🙂 Ganga

qa.q: When did Farhan start rubbing his eyes and tugging his ear?
qa.a: Around midday, just before nap time.

qa.q: What might Farhan's eye rubbing and ear tugging mean, and how did Ganga decide?
qa.a: It most likely meant he was sleepy, and Ganga looked at the whole picture: nap time, lunch eaten, cool skin and a noisy room. The ear tug could have another cause, so she watches whether it continues.

qa.q: What should Ganga do if the ear tugging continues?
qa.a: She should tell his parents so they can check with the doctor, since it may be more than tiredness.

qa.q: How might Farhan's parents feel on reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that Ganga looked carefully and told them, and know what to watch for.

grounding: A toddler rubs his eyes and pulls his ear, an ambiguous cue that the caregiver checks against the whole situation.

passage: The bus ride from town had taken all afternoon, and by the evening meal Avni, two, was tugging at her right ear and rubbing her eyes with her fists. Jomon looked at her: she had eaten little, the radio was loud and she had been awake since dawn. He turned the radio off, lifted her on his lap and rocked her. She pressed her face into his shirt and was asleep in a few minutes. He decided that if the tugging carried on the next day, he would ask the clinic nurse.

qa.q: What did Jomon switch off?
qa.a: The radio.

qa.q: What did Jomon think Avni's ear tugging and eye rubbing meant?
qa.a: He thought she was tired after the long bus ride, since she had eaten little and been awake since dawn. He still kept in mind that ear tugging can have other causes.

qa.q: What would Jomon do if the tugging kept going?
qa.a: He would ask the clinic nurse the next day, as it might be something more than tiredness.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when he turned off the radio?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved as the noise stopped, and safe in his lap. 🙂

grounding: A toddler rubs eyes and tugs an ear when sleepy, and the father checks the wider context instead of relying on one sign.

passage: Rehana, two, always sat on the sofa at six o'clock with her thumb in her mouth, twirling a lock of hair with the other hand, eyes half shut. Her aunt tutted. “She's too big for that. Stop it.” Jyoti touched her daughter's foot gently. “She's tired. It settles her, and she'll drop it herself.” Rehana leaned against the cushion and sighed, and her hand stopped twirling. Jyoti put a blanket over her and switched off the loud television.

qa.q: What time did Rehana usually sit on the sofa?
qa.a: At six o'clock.

qa.q: What does the thumb and hair twirling seem to do for Rehana?
qa.a: It seems to comfort her and help her settle at a tired time of day. It could also show worry, though the sigh suggests she was simply tired.

qa.q: How did Jyoti handle her sister's comment?
qa.a: She defended Rehana calmly and did not shame her, then made the room quieter. She could gently offer other comforts too.

qa.q: How might Rehana's aunt see it?
qa.a: She may have grown up believing that habits like this should be stopped, and may feel worried Rehana will never grow out of it.

grounding: A toddler sucks a thumb and twirls hair when tired, a typical comfort that needs no shaming.

passage:
“Eshaan, come here,” said Chinmay. The living room was full of relatives, all talking loudly.
Eshaan stood at the edge of the sofa with one thumb in his mouth, his other hand rubbing the corner of his blanket.
“You've had a long day, haven't you?”
Eshaan nodded and stroked the blanket again.
“Do you want to sit with me?”
He climbed up and leaned on Chinmay's arm.
An aunt whispered, “He still sucks his thumb?”
“He does,” said Chinmay lightly. “It helps him.”

qa.q: What was Eshaan rubbing with one hand?
qa.a: The corner of his blanket.

qa.q: Why do you think Eshaan sucked his thumb and rubbed the blanket?
qa.a: He was probably tired and a bit overwhelmed by the crowd of relatives, so he comforted himself. It might also be a habit he uses at any change.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do to help Eshaan through the gathering?
qa.a: He could find a quiet corner for a break and keep Eshaan's blanket close.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel when Chinmay replies to the aunt?
qa.a: He may not understand the words, but feels calm because his father is not upset by his comfort habit.

grounding: A toddler sucks a thumb and strokes a blanket when tired or overwhelmed, a normal comfort that needs no shaming.

passage: Nursery note, Wednesday. After her nap, Mehak, two, walked straight over to me, climbed into my lap and pressed her cheek against my chest without a word. She stayed there quietly for a few minutes, holding my finger. Later I opened my arms for a hug during a game and she stepped back and shook her head, so I smiled and went on with the game. She came back to my side ten minutes later on her own. 🙂 Disha

qa.q: What did Mehak hold while she sat in Disha's lap?
qa.a: Disha's finger.

qa.q: What might Mehak's cuddling after her nap show, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It probably shows she wanted comfort and closeness after waking. She might also have been simply sleepy.

qa.q: Why was it good that Disha accepted Mehak stepping back?
qa.a: She respected Mehak's no to a hug, which teaches Mehak that her signals count, and Mehak returned by herself later.

qa.q: How might Mehak's parents feel reading this?
qa.a: They may be glad she has a safe adult to cuddle and that her wish to say no was respected.

grounding: A toddler climbs into a lap to seek comfort and closeness, and the adult respects it when the child steps back.

passage: The power went out at dusk, and the small house turned dark except for the lantern. Ritu, two, who had been playing with her clay bullocks, dropped them and scrambled into her mother Kalyani's lap. She wound her arms round her neck and burrowed her face in the folds of her saree. Kalyani wrapped her in the shawl and rubbed her back. Ritu went quiet and slowly loosened her hold. When the light returned, she stayed where she was for a long while.

qa.q: What did Ritu drop when the power went out?
qa.a: Her clay bullocks.

qa.q: What does Ritu's climbing into her mother's lap suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy in the dark and wanted comfort. She might also have wanted her mother's attention, but the tight hold and quiet point to fear.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do the next time the lights go out?
qa.a: She could keep the lantern nearby and hold Ritu close, and keep speaking softly so Ritu knows she is there.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel holding her?
qa.a: She may feel tender and needed, and relieved that Ritu turns to her for comfort. 🤍

grounding: A toddler climbs into a lap and cuddles to seek comfort and closeness in the dark, and warm touch helps.

passage:
“Pranav, no! Gentle hands,” said Ishita.
Pranav had shoved Dev off the sandpit edge because Dev had taken the yellow truck. He stood red-faced, fists clenched, shouting “Mine!”
“You're angry. That's your truck, and Dev took it.” She held his hands. “But pushing hurts. Use your words: ‘Mine, please.’”
“Mine puh.”
“Good. Dev, can you give it back?”
Dev handed it over, and Pranav took it, then patted Dev's arm, unsure.
“Gentle,” Ishita said. “Like that.”

qa.q: What did Pranav push Dev over?
qa.a: The yellow truck that Dev had taken.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he pushed Dev, and what was he missing?
qa.a: He felt angry and strongly wanted his truck, and he did not yet have words to say “no” or “mine” calmly. It was not cruelty.

qa.q: What could Ishita do next time to prevent a push?
qa.a: She could stay near, step in early to help the children take turns and remind Pranav of his words.

qa.q: How might Dev feel after being pushed?
qa.a: He may feel startled and hurt, so a gentle pat from Pranav helps him feel safe again.

grounding: A toddler pushes when frustrated and lacks words, and the parent sets a calm limit, names the feeling and teaches gentle hands.

passage: Toddler room note, Thursday. When Bilal took the wooden blocks Parveen was stacking, Parveen, two, hit his arm with her open hand and shouted, then grabbed the block back. I moved close, crouched and said, “You wanted your blocks. You were cross. But no hitting.” I held her hand and stroked it gently on Bilal's arm: “Gentle.” Then I gave Bilal his own blocks. Parveen watched, calmer. I will keep this calm approach and model gentle touch. 🙂 Imran

qa.q: What did Parveen hit Bilal for?
qa.a: Because he took the blocks she was stacking.

qa.q: What does Parveen's hitting show about how she felt?
qa.a: It shows anger and a strong wish to keep her blocks, since she did not have words for “no” or “mine”. It was not meant to be cruel.

qa.q: What worked well in how Imran handled the incident?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named her feeling, set a firm limit and showed gentle touch, then made sure Bilal had his own blocks.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel after the incident?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and sore, and Imran's attention shows him he will be looked after.

grounding: A toddler hits when frustrated and lacks words, and the teacher sets a calm limit, names the feeling and teaches gentle hands.

subtype: Approaching and staying near a caregiver [Expressing]
passage: I sat on the park bench watching a toddler named Uday explore near the slide, and I noticed something. Every few minutes he stopped, turned and looked for his mother Pallavi on the next bench. She lifted a hand; he grinned and toddled off again. Once he ran back, patted her knee and left. I can't know what he felt, but he seemed to use her as a home base. When he wandered towards the gate, Pallavi stood up and walked over to him.

qa.q: Where was Pallavi sitting?
qa.a: On the next bench in the park.

qa.q: What does the narrator think Uday's looking back shows?
qa.a: She thinks he wanted reassurance that his mother was still there, using her as a base. She does not claim to know what he felt.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi stand up when Uday went toward the gate?
qa.a: He was heading somewhere less safe, and at his age he needs an adult to watch and step in. She might also just want to keep him within sight.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel as she watches him roam and return?
qa.a: She may feel proud that he explores and glad that he checks in, while staying alert to danger.

grounding: A toddler stays within sight of a parent, returns for reassurance and explores, seen by an observer, with the parent supervising near the gate.

subtype: Approaching and staying near a caregiver [Expressing]
passage: Monday: at the park, Mehak, two, stayed close to Sonali's bench, digging in the sand within arm's reach, glancing up now and then. Tuesday: she walked to the slide and looked back three times, waiting for Sonali's nod before climbing. Wednesday: she ran further, laughing, then hurried back for a quick hug and dashed off again. Then she headed straight for the gate without looking back, so Sonali quickly moved beside her and took her hand. “Let's explore this way.”

qa.q: What did Mehak do on Tuesday before climbing the slide?
qa.a: She looked back at Sonali several times and waited for her nod.

qa.q: What might Mehak's looking back and quick hug mean she felt?
qa.a: They suggest she wanted reassurance and feels safe with Sonali, which lets her explore further. It might also be simple habit.

qa.q: Why did Sonali step in on Wednesday?
qa.a: Mehak headed to the gate without checking back, so she needed supervision to stay safe.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel over these three days?
qa.a: She may feel glad and proud as Mehak grows braver, and watchful as the distances grow. 🙂

grounding: A toddler stays near a parent, returns for reassurance and explores further, and a child who wanders off without checking back needs supervision.

passage: In the lift of their building, a new neighbour smiled at Imran, two, and said, “What a nice little man!” Imran twisted round, buried his face in his mother Usha's coat and held her leg. “It's okay,” Usha murmured, without pushing him. The neighbour stayed a step back, talking to Usha about the building. By the second floor Imran peeked out at the neighbour, then turned away again, but when she waved, he lifted a hand for a second.

qa.q: Where did the meeting take place?
qa.a: In the lift of their building.

qa.q: What does Imran's turning to Usha suggest he feels about the stranger?
qa.a: It suggests wariness of someone new, and he looked out again out of curiosity. It could also be that the small crowded lift made him uneasy.

qa.q: What did the neighbour do that helped?
qa.a: She kept a gentle distance and spoke to Usha, letting Imran decide when to look.

qa.q: How might Usha feel about Imran's reaction?
qa.a: She may feel a little embarrassed but also understanding, and glad the neighbour was patient. 🙂

grounding: A toddler turns away from a stranger and toward a parent, showing wariness, and the adult waits and keeps a gentle distance.

passage:
“Chaitanya, this is Uncle Ravi. Say hello,” said Lalit.
Chaitanya turned her whole body away and held on to Lalit's shirt.
“She's shy today,” Lalit told Ravi.
“No problem. Hello, Chaitanya,” said Ravi, and sat down on the far side of the room.
“Ravi is very nice,” said Lalit.
“No,” said Chaitanya into his shoulder.
“That's okay. You can just watch.”
A few minutes later she peeked at Ravi's shoes and said, “Big.”

qa.q: Where did Ravi sit?
qa.a: On the far side of the room.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's turning away and saying “No” suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests wariness of a new person, not rudeness. Peeking at his shoes later shows some curiosity was growing.

qa.q: What could Lalit and Ravi do next?
qa.a: They could keep a distance, talk about something interesting like Ravi's shoes and let her come closer herself.

qa.q: How might Ravi feel about the reaction?
qa.a: He may feel a little awkward, but knowing Chaitanya is wary helps him stay relaxed and patient.

grounding: A toddler turns away from a stranger and toward a parent, showing wariness, and the adults let her approach in her own time.

passage: In a flat in Warsaw, Marek draped a scarf over his face and yanked it away. Bilal, two, gave a squeal of laughter and reached for the scarf. Marek hid again and Bilal giggled harder, eyes shining. Then Marek tickled his tummy and the giggles came in bursts, with wriggling. When Marek suddenly leapt up and roared like a lion, Bilal laughed a little, but his eyes were wide and his hand went out for Marek's sleeve. Marek dropped to the floor. “Too much? Come here.” Bilal climbed into his lap.

qa.q: What did Marek use for the peekaboo game?
qa.a: A scarf.

qa.q: Why did Marek stop the lion roar, and what did he notice in Bilal?
qa.a: Bilal's laugh was small, his eyes were wide and he grabbed his father's sleeve, suggesting nervous surprise more than fun. He could have been enjoying it, but Marek chose to check.

qa.q: What could Marek try next?
qa.a: He could go back to gentle games, watch for signs of comfort and stop or slow down when Bilal shows worry.

qa.q: How might Bilal see his father's change of game?
qa.a: He may feel understood and safe because his father noticed his worry without being asked. 🙂

grounding: A toddler giggles at peekaboo and tickles and laughs more when a caregiver joins in, while nervous surprise laughter calls for checking cues of comfort.

passage: On the train platform I watched Lakshmi, about two, being tickled by her mother Sangeeta on a bench. She laughed, wriggled and pushed her mother's hand back for more. Then Sangeeta lifted her high over her head. Lakshmi laughed too, but her eyes were wide and she gripped Sangeeta's wrists. I don't know what she was feeling, but Sangeeta brought her down at once and said, “Tickle again?” Lakshmi's laugh became easy and she settled into her lap.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do when she wanted more tickling?
qa.a: She pushed her mother's hand back for more.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta bring Lakshmi down, and what does the narrator think?
qa.a: Lakshmi's wide eyes and tight grip on her wrists showed the laugh was mixed with alarm. The narrator admits she cannot know what Lakshmi felt.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do with what she noticed?
qa.a: She could keep games low to the ground for now, watch Lakshmi's face and stop if the laugh sounds nervous.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi feel when her mother lowers her?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and safe, and glad that her mother stopped when she was unsure. 🙂

grounding: A toddler laughs with tickles and joins in play, but a nervous laugh with wide eyes is spotted by an observer and the mother checks.

subtype: Laughing at a fall or a shock [Mismatch]
passage:
“Lalremsiami, careful!” said Shalini, as her daughter tumbled off the low cushion pile and landed on the rug. For a second Lalremsiami lay very still. Then she burst out laughing, looking straight at her mother.
“Bump! Are you okay?”
“Bump,” said Lalremsiami, still laughing.
Shalini crouched and ran her hands over her arms and legs. “Nothing hurts?”
Lalremsiami shook her head and got up to climb again.
“Slowly this time,” said Shalini.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami land on?
qa.a: The rug, after tumbling off the low cushion pile.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami laugh after falling, and what could it mean?
qa.a: She was probably checking her mother's face and may have felt relieved or surprised. It could also be copying, but she was not being unkind or callous.

qa.q: What did Shalini do that helped?
qa.a: She stayed calm, checked her arms and legs and named the bump, showing it was a safe moment.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when she first sees the fall?
qa.a: She may feel a jolt of fear, then relief when she hears the laugh. 🙂

grounding: A toddler laughs after a fall while looking at her parent, which can be relief or confusion, and the calm parent shows the moment was safe.

subtype: Laughing at a fall or a shock [Mismatch]
passage: Toddler room note, Monday. A balloon burst near the window. Chandrika, two, jumped, went still and then giggled, looking straight at me. I smiled and said, “That was a loud pop! Are you all right?” She giggled again, then leaned against my knee. I checked that she was not upset and gave her a squeeze. I do not think she was being callous. She was probably deciding from my face whether it was safe. 🙂 Amandeep

qa.q: What made Chandrika jump?
qa.a: A balloon that burst near the window.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's giggle and look at Amandeep suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was surprised and checking whether it was safe, then relieved when Amandeep smiled. It could also be copying, but she was not being callous.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do if Chandrika's giggle turned to tears?
qa.a: She could hold her, name the scare and let her take her time before returning to play.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's mother react if she heard the story?
qa.a: She might worry the laugh was unkind, but Amandeep's note would help her see it as a child reading a grown-up's calm.

grounding: A toddler laughs after a scare while looking to an adult for a reaction, which can be relief or confusion, and the calm response shows it was safe.

subtype: Bawling from distress or unmet need [Expressing]
passage: Nursery note, Friday. At half past four Baljeet, two, began to bawl at the door, loud and shaking, tears streaming. He had not eaten his snack, he had skipped his nap and a door had banged nearby. I picked him up straight away, spoke softly and gave him water and a banana. He cried for a while longer, then his breathing slowed, and he rested his head on my shoulder. The crying was the only alarm he had. 🙂 Lokesh

qa.q: What did Lokesh give Baljeet after picking him up?
qa.a: Water and a banana.

qa.q: What was Baljeet probably feeling behind his crying?
qa.a: It seems to be a mix of hunger, tiredness and a fright from the banging door. His need was real, not a trick.

qa.q: Why does a quick, calm response matter?
qa.a: It teaches him that distress can be relieved and that an adult will come, which builds trust.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel relieved that he was comforted quickly and that Lokesh looked at the whole day, not just the crying.

grounding: A toddler bawls from hunger, tiredness and fear, the strongest alarm signal, and a quick calm response builds trust.

subtype: Bawling from distress or unmet need [Expressing]
passage: At dusk, Ankita, two, sat at the edge of the courtyard and began to bawl, her mouth wide, her face red and her hands clenched. Her father Francis, who had just come in from the field, put down his tools. It was past her usual mealtime and the day had been hot. He lifted her, wiped her face and offered a bowl of warm rice and milk. Between sobs she ate. Slowly her wails softened into hiccups, and she leaned into his chest.

qa.q: What did Francis offer Ankita?
qa.a: A bowl of warm rice and milk.

qa.q: What might Ankita's bawling have shown?
qa.a: She was probably hungry and tired after a hot day, as the timing and her eating suggest. It could also include being upset that her father was late.

qa.q: What could Francis do to prevent this?
qa.a: He could keep a snack ready when he expects to be late and rest with her after a long day.

qa.q: How might Francis feel hearing her cry?
qa.a: He may feel worried and urgent, and relieved to see food calming her. 🙂

grounding: A toddler bawls loudly with hunger and fatigue, and a calm, quick, soothing response relieves the distress.

subtype: Crying as a signal of need [Expressing]
passage: In their flat in London, Hana, two, cried in three ways that afternoon. First a thin, whining cry as she rubbed her eyes, which her mother Nkechi knew meant sleepy. Then a sharp, loud scream when the tower fell, with clenched fists. Later a wobbly, trembling cry when the vacuum cleaner started. Nkechi answered each differently: a cot and lullaby, a hug and a new tower, and switching off the vacuum. Hana's cries all stopped in time. Nkechi said, “She's telling me, not tricking me.”

qa.q: How many different cries did Hana have that afternoon?
qa.a: Three: a thin whining cry, a sharp scream and a wobbly trembling cry.

qa.q: What did each of Hana's cries mean, in Nkechi's reading?
qa.a: The whining cry meant sleepiness, the scream meant frustration at the fallen tower, and the trembling one meant fear of the vacuum. Nkechi could have been wrong about one, but she checked each in context.

qa.q: What could Nkechi do if she is unsure what a cry means?
qa.a: She could look at what happened just before, check the basics such as hunger and tiredness, and comfort first.

qa.q: How might Hana feel when her cries are answered?
qa.a: She may feel safe and learn to trust that someone hears her, so she cries less over time. 🙂

grounding: A toddler cries from tiredness, frustration and fear with different-sounding cries, and warm prompt responses show it is communication, not manipulation.

subtype: Crying as a signal of need [Expressing]
passage: At the bus stop I watched a boy, Pranav, about two, start to cry in his pushchair. His mother Ishita bent down and checked in a calm order: she offered water, touched his forehead lightly, looked at his feet and asked, “Hungry? Tired?” The cry was rising and hoarse. When she handed him a rice cracker, the cry broke into a hiccup and stopped. I can't say for sure what it was, but she treated it like a message, not a nuisance.

qa.q: What did Ishita hand to Pranav that stopped the crying?
qa.a: A rice cracker.

qa.q: What did Ishita seem to think Pranav's crying meant?
qa.a: She treated it as a message about a need, and the cracker working suggests he was hungry. The narrator admits she cannot say for sure.

qa.q: What could Ishita do if the cracker had not worked?
qa.a: She could try comfort, check his clothes and keep looking for the cause, and see a doctor if the crying seems unusual or worries her.

qa.q: How might other people at the bus stop react?
qa.a: Some may feel irritated by the crying, while others recognise how hard it is and feel sympathy for Ishita.

grounding: A toddler cries from a need such as hunger, and an observer sees the mother treat it as communication and respond warmly.
